what_its_for: Vorapaxar is a blood-thinning medicine that helps prevent serious heart problems like heart attacks and strokes in people who have already had a heart attack or have poor circulation in their legs (peripheral artery disease). It works by stopping blood platelets from clumping together and forming dangerous clots.
how_to_take: Take vorapaxar by mouth with or without food. Swallow the tablet whole. Try to take it at the same time every day to help you remember. Do not stop taking this medicine without talking to your doctor first, even if you feel fine — stopping suddenly can raise your risk of a serious heart event.
dosing: The usual dose is one 2.08 mg tablet taken by mouth once daily. Always take the dose your doctor prescribed. Do not take more or less than directed.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember on the same day. If it is already the next day, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Never take two doses on the same day to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store vorapaxar at room temperature between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it in the original container with the lid tightly closed. Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush medicines down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about the best way to dispose of unused medicine.
what_to_avoid: Avoid activities that could cause cuts or injury, since this medicine makes it harder for your blood to clot. Use a soft toothbrush and electric razor to reduce bleeding risks. Tell all of your doctors and your dentist that you take this medicine before any procedure or surgery. Avoid taking aspirin, ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin), naproxen (Aleve), or other NSAIDs unless your doctor approves, as they increase bleeding risk. Do not take certain antifungal medicines like itraconazole or ketoconazole, or certain antibiotics like clarithromycin, without checking with your doctor, as they can raise vorapaxar levels in your blood to dangerous levels.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you notice: unusual or uncontrolled bleeding (cuts that won't stop bleeding), coughing or vomiting blood, blood in your urine or stool (pink, red, or black/tarry stools), heavy menstrual bleeding, sudden severe headache, dizziness, weakness, or vision changes (possible signs of bleeding in the brain), or if you are planning any surgery, dental procedure, or medical procedure. Also call your doctor if you feel very faint or have unexplained bruising.
when_it_works: Vorapaxar starts working to reduce platelet activity within a few hours of your first dose. However, because it is a long-acting medicine, its full protective effect builds up over time with regular daily use. It may take several weeks to reach its maximum effect in your body. Do not stop taking it just because you do not notice immediate changes — it is working in the background to protect your heart and blood vessels.
special_populations: Do NOT take vorapaxar if you have ever had a stroke or a mini-stroke (TIA) — it significantly increases the risk of brain bleeding in these patients. This medicine is not recommended for use during pregnancy or breastfeeding; talk to your doctor about safer options. Vorapaxar has not been studied in children and should not be used in patients under 18. Older adults (65 and over) may have a higher risk of bleeding and should be monitored closely. People with severe liver disease should not use this medicine. If you have kidney problems, tell your doctor, though dose adjustment is usually not needed.
